after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Find the arc length of the polar curve $r=5-5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$

*Hint: You may wish to use the following identity: $\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\sqrt{\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}.$*
after.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=5-5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{(5-5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{25-50\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +25{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +25{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{25-50\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +25}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{50-50\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{50}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall the identity for $\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2}):$

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\sqrt{\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}
$$

Therefore, using $x=\theta $ in the previous identity, the integral can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =\sqrt{50}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{50}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={-10\cdot 2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}))|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =-20(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})-\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-20(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-1) \\  & =20-10\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

a
∫−π/4π/41+2sin⁡(2θ)+4cos2⁡(2θ)dθ
b
∫0π/21+2sin⁡(2θ)+4cos2⁡(2θ)dθ
c
∫0π/22+2sin⁡(2θ)+3cos2⁡(2θ)dθ
d

e

decision.explanation: The polar arc length integrand is √(r²+(dr/dθ)²). Since dr/dθ=2cos(2θ), its squared value is (1+sin(2θ))²+4cos²(2θ)=2+2sin(2θ)+3cos²(2θ). With the given bounds −π/4 to π/4, this is option d.

Which of the following integrals gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )$ for $-\,\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}$ (shown in blue in the  diagram above)?
after.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta )+4{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+1+3{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{2+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+3{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

b
∫0π/21+2sin⁡(2θ)+4cos2⁡(2θ)dθ
c
∫0π/22+2sin⁡(2θ)+3cos2⁡(2θ)dθ
d
∫−π/4π/42+2sin⁡(2θ)+3cos2⁡(2θ)dθ
e
∫−π/4π/42+4sin⁡(2θ)+2cos2⁡(2θ)dθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The arc length L of a polar curve r=r(θ) is given by

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=1+sin⁡(2θ), we have

drdθ=2cos⁡(2θ).

Therefore, the arc length is

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫−π/4π/4(1+sin⁡(2θ))2+(2cos⁡(2θ))2dθ=∫−π/4π/41+2sin⁡(2θ)+sin2⁡(2θ)+4cos2⁡(2θ)dθ=∫−π/4π/41+2sin⁡(2θ)+1+3cos2⁡(2θ)dθ=∫−π/4π/42+2sin⁡(2θ)+3cos2⁡(2θ)dθ.

Which of the following integrals gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )$ for $-\,\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}$ (shown in blue in the  diagram above)?
content.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta )+4{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+1+3{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{2+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+3{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve r=5+sin⁡(5θ) for 0≤θ≤π (shown in blue in the diagram above).

a
∫0π25+10sin⁡(5θ)+25cos2⁡(5θ)dθ
b
∫0π26+10sin⁡(5θ)+24cos2⁡(5θ)dθ
c
∫0π26+5sin⁡(5θ)+25cos2⁡(5θ)dθ
d
∫0π26+5sin⁡(5θ)+24cos2⁡(5θ)dθ
e
∫0π24+10sin⁡(5θ)+25cos2⁡(5θ)dθ
Submit

decision.explanation: Polar arc length is ∫√(r²+(r′)²) dθ. Here r′=5cos(5θ), so r²+(r′)²=25+10sin(5θ)+sin²(5θ)+25cos²(5θ)=26+10sin(5θ)+24cos²(5θ). Integrating from 0 to π gives option b.

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=5+\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta )$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi $ (shown in blue in the diagram above).
after.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=5+\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(5+\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta ))^{2}+(5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{25+10\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta )+{sin}^{2}⁡(5\theta )+25{cos}^{2}⁡(5\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{25+10\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta )+1+24{cos}^{2}⁡(5\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{26+10\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta )+24{cos}^{2}⁡(5\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve r=5+sin⁡(5θ) for 0≤θ≤π (shown in blue in the diagram above).

a
∫0π25+10sin⁡(5θ)+25cos2⁡(5θ)dθ
b
∫0π26+10sin⁡(5θ)+24cos2⁡(5θ)dθ
c
∫0π26+5sin⁡(5θ)+25cos2⁡(5θ)dθ
d
∫0π26+5sin⁡(5θ)+24cos2⁡(5θ)dθ
e
∫0π24+10sin⁡(5θ)+25cos2⁡(5θ)dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The arc length L of a polar curve r=r(θ) is given by

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=5+sin⁡(5θ), we have drdθ=5cos⁡(5θ).

Therefore, the arc length is

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π(5+sin⁡(5θ))2+(5cos⁡(5θ))2dθ=∫0π25+10sin⁡(5θ)+sin2⁡(5θ)+25cos2⁡(5θ)dθ=∫0π25+10sin⁡(5θ)+1+24cos2⁡(5θ)dθ=∫0π26+10sin⁡(5θ)+24cos2⁡(5θ)dθ.

content.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$
